To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) naive Bayes is optimal if there is no dependence among the attributes, and (2) naive Bayes can also be optimal even if there is dependence among the attributes.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that, essentially, how the local dependences of all attributes distribute in each class, and how the dependences work together, consistently or inconsistently, plays a crucial role in determining the performance of naive Bayesian classifiers.
we provide a theoretical analysis on why naive Bayes works.

, we provide a novel explanation on why naive Bayes is surprisingly competitive in classification, and we propose and prove a set of sufficient and necessary conditions on which naive Bayes is optimal.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, the surprising classification performance of Naive Bayess is not only due to the fact that it can handle complex data, or due to the fact it is simple, or due to that it is a probabilistic classifier. Rather

, the surprising good classification performance of naive bayes is due to the fact that the local dependence of each node is evenly distributed in classes, or the local dependencies cancel each other out.
, no matter how complex the dependence structure is, naive Bayes is still optimal when the dependences among the attributes distribute evenly in classes.
